subject: Culture
title: Wearing Black
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Wearing Black.

hook.text: Queen Victoria wore black mourning clothes for 40 years after Prince Albert died. She set the fashion for grief.

buildup.text: Black mourning dress became a strict code in Victorian England. Different fabrics marked stages of grief.

discovery.text: Not all cultures mourn in black. In India and China, white is the mourning color. In Egypt, it was historically yellow.

twist.text: The black mourning industry was enormous. Special shops sold only funeral clothing, veils, and accessories.

climax.text: Modern Western funerals are relaxing the dress code. Some families now request bright colors to celebrate life.

punchline.text: The color of grief is a cultural choice, not a universal truth.

quiz.question: How long did Queen Victoria wear mourning black?

details.summary: Wearing black for mourning is a Western tradition that feels universal but is culturally specific. Queen Victoria's 40-year mourning period after Prince Albert's death cemented black as grief's color. Before and beyond the West, mourning colors range from white to red to yellow.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding that mourning black is a cultural choice, not a universal instinct, prevents ethnocentric assumptions about how grief should look across different cultures.
takeaways: Queen Victoria popularized extended black mourning dress
Black mourning dress became standard only in the 19th century
Many cultures use white, red, or other colors for mourning

faq.question: How long did Victorian mourning dress last?
faq.answer: Victorian mourning had strict stages. 'Full mourning' (all black, no jewelry) lasted one year for a spouse. 'Second mourning' (black with some trim) lasted nine months. 'Ordinary mourning' (grey and muted colors) lasted three to six months.

faq.question: Did people always wear black for mourning in the West?
faq.answer: No. Medieval European mourning included white and grey. Roman mourners wore dark (but not always black) toga pulla. Black became dominant in the 16th century and was standardized by the Victorian era.
